name: Palenquero

catalog_citation: Hualde, José Ignacio & Armin Schwegler. 2008. Intonation in Palenquero. Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 23(1): 1-31. Authors' 46-pp. preprint (header 'Published in Journal of Pidgin and Creole Languages 23.1 (2008): 1-31'), Hualde's UIUC page via the Internet Archive.
catalog_locator: Preprint p. 4 (sec. 1, review of Bickerton & Escalante 1970: 257 and Patiño 1983: 109-110); p. 9 (sec. 4.1 'Pitch accents'); p. 25 (sec. 4.4 'The long nuclear fall'); pp. 35-36 (sec. 5 'Summary and discussion of origins'). Published pagination differs (Lipski 2010 cites the 'accentual language' sentence at p. 25).
catalog_quote: Bickerton & Escalante claim that in Palenquero, “final-syllable accent is a matter of high tone rather than stress”, and that “there are some pairs, such as kusina ‘kitchen’, kusiná ‘to cook’, which are only tonally distinguished” (1970: 257). While acknowledging the existence of striking intonational patterns, Patiño (1983: 109-110) denies the existence of contrastive lexical tone in Palenquero, preferring to interpret word-level prosody in terms of stress [...] In the Palenquero corpus that we have examined, declarative sentences typically exhibit a high tone on every stressed syllable (that is, on every syllable that would be stressed in the Spanish cognate word), without any displacement of the peak. [...] (but most words are, in fact, paroxytonic). [...] All other words would bear a lexical H-tone on one of the syllables, which is again the stressed syllable of the corresponding Spanish word, in the lexicon of Spanish origin. [...] Typologically, however, Palenquero is still closer to being an accentual language than a tone language since (a) there can be only one H-toned syllable per word, and (b) every lexical word has a H-toned syllable (there are no toneless words, except for some function words). [...] In the final analysis, we find ourselves in agreement with Patiño’s (1983, 2002) position that Palenquero is best analyzed as an accentual language, rather than as a language with lexical tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Palenquero has Spanish-type lexical (contrastive) word stress: each lexical word has exactly one stressed syllable, located on the syllable that is stressed in the Spanish etymon (so mostly penultimate, with oxytones e.g. r-less infinitives kusiná, miná, kasá and stressed enclitics -nú, -mí, -bó); the stressed syllable is realised with a level high pitch (and lengthening), unstressed syllables low; the authors (with Patiño 1983) classify the system as accentual rather than lexical-tone. Stress minimal pairs: kusína 'kitchen' / kusiná 'to cook' (Bickerton & Escalante), mína/miná, cása/casá (Lipski 2010), ['ka.lo] 'soup' / [ka.'lo] 'heat' (Lopez-Barrios 2024).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; explicitly 'only one H-toned syllable per word'.
new_statements.exceptions: Some function words are unstressed/toneless (as in Spanish); words of Bantu origin (moná, lumbalú, ngómbe) carry their own marked stress; phrase-final H may be downstepped or stay level without L% (intonational, not lexical). Bickerton & Escalante 1970 had described final accent as 'high tone rather than stress'; Hualde & Schwegler and Patiño reject a lexical-tone analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress inferred from an intonation study of connected speech (older-generation, conservative speakers recorded 1985-88 and later); H aligns within the stressed syllable in all sentence positions, so citation-form and phrase-medial stress coincide.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes conservative (older-generation) Palenquero of San Basilio de Palenque = Glottolog pale1260 / ISO pln; no dialect divisions. Not to be confused with local Spanish ('kateyano') of Palenque, which Correa 2017 and Lopez-Barrios treat separately.

tone_statements.quote: In their analysis of Palenquero intonation, Hualde and Schwegler (2008) observe that accented syllables receive a level H tone, and lexical words have at most one H tone per word. The authors conclude (p. 25) that “Palenquero is best analyzed as an accentual language, rather than as a language with lexical tone.” The present study, while essentially grounded in Hualde and Schwegler’s conclusion, offers more detailed data on a particular configuration that may signal a final vestige (or the incipient development) of a phonologically distinctive tone.

sources.note: Word-level prosody is accentual (not lexical tone): every lexical word has exactly one prominent (H-toned) syllable, which is the syllable stressed in the corresponding Spanish word; most words are paroxytonic; stress-based minimal pairs exist (kusína 'kitchen' vs kusiná 'to cook', citing Bickerton & Escalante 1970:257); reviews Montes 1962, Patiño 1983 (stress, not tone), Moñino ('tonal-accentual').
